source: Chrysikou & Weisberg (2005) Following the wrong footsteps: fixation effects of pictorial examples in a design problem-solving task. JEP:LMC 31(5):1134-1148
finding: Two experiments with non-expert designers and pictorial examples that contained problem features. People followed the examples even when they held inappropriate elements. A defixation condition (same problematic example plus an instruction to avoid its problem elements) reduced the fixation effect.
numbers: Exp 1: N=89 think-aloud participants in 3 conditions (control; fixation = problematic example with its problems described; defixation = problematic example with instruction to avoid the problem elements). 176 verbal protocols coded for reasons for citing the example. Exp 2: N=60 non-verbalizing participants. Per-condition copy counts are NOT in the abstract; full text not reached (APA paywall).
quote: the fixation effects can be diminished with the use of defixating instructions
limits: Abstract only. Copy counts and effect sizes unread. The defixation arm is an informed-example design, so it is not a clean replication of Jansson-Smith's warning condition.
agent_relevance: Primary evidence that an explicit avoid-X instruction CAN cut copying in people. It contradicts the earlier reading (K02) that warnings never work. Test the avoid-X instruction in context for an LLM; do not assume it fails.

source: Jansson & Smith (1991) Design fixation. Design Studies 12(1):3-11
finding: Crossref confirms the record (title, journal, pages) but gives no abstract. Founding numbers (N per experiment, copy counts, warning condition) still could not be read; the paper is paywalled and no open copy was reachable. Open-access papers only cite it for 'subsequent solutions replicate features of the known solution' (PMC8548374) and note that Exp 4 used professional engineers (PMC6357673).
numbers: None obtained. Fixation is scored as presence or absence of each repeated example feature (PMC6357673); over half of the studies in Vasconcelos and Crilly 2016 used this replicated-features measure.
limits: Gap 3 stays open for the exact numbers. Every claim about Jansson-Smith in claims.jsonl remains second-hand.
agent_relevance: Do not quote Jansson-Smith numbers in schema docs. Cite only the direction (examples raise feature copying) and mark it second-hand.

source: Sio, Kotovsky & Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes. Design Studies 39:70-99
finding: Only a search-result summary of the abstract was seen (the web search budget ran out and the open TU Delft copy could not be reached). Examples narrowed the range of ideas but made them more novel; idea quality rose with the degree of copying; facilitation of novelty and quality was larger with fewer and less common examples; one single uncommon example helped most.
numbers: N = 43 studies (stated). No effect sizes, confidence intervals, heterogeneity or moderator coefficients were obtained.
limits: Search snippet, not the paper. The 'quality rises with copying' point is new relative to K05 but unverified.
agent_relevance: Design rule stays: show at most one rare example, never several common ones. Gap 2 stays open: effect sizes unread.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin 135(1):94-120
finding: Positive incubation effect overall. Divergent-thinking tasks gain more than linguistic or visual insight tasks. Longer preparation gives a bigger effect. A high-demand filler task shrinks the effect. For linguistic insight problems a low-demand filler beat rest.
numbers: Overall effect size and k are not in the abstract; only the direction of moderators was read.
limits: Abstract only. Human breaks, not model context. The result that divergent thinking benefits most is the one relevant to ideation.
agent_relevance: Closest human basis for a break operator: first work long enough to build up a set, then switch away (reset or an unrelated low-load step), then return. A truncation or fresh-context restart is the agent analogue; it is untested.

source: Exposure to Ideas, Evaluation Apprehension, and Incubation Intervals in Collaborative Idea Generation (2019) Frontiers in Psychology 10:1459
finding: Three experiments on dyads. Seeing others' ideas cut the number and categories of ideas without changing novelty. The harm did not appear in the first 10 minutes; it grew over time. Two incubation breaks (relax or an unrelated task) removed the deficit. The authors explain it by selective forgetting of redundant ideas (Smith and Blankenship 1991).
numbers: Exp 3, idea count in the last 10 min: exposed-immediate vs exposed-relax mean difference -3.21 (p=.003); vs exposed-task -2.38 (p=.029); exposed-relax vs exposed-task 0.83 (p=.431); non-exposed vs exposed-immediate 1.61 (p=.136, not significant). Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Social exposure to partners' ideas, not design examples. Small effects, p values uncorrected, sample sizes unread.
agent_relevance: Supports two agent tests. (1) Timing: the cost of exposure shows up late, not at the first idea, so judge fixation across the whole run. (2) Break: a context reset after a stretch of ideation should drop the redundant ideas. Delayed exposure (gap 6) is only half-supported: this paper compares break types after exposure, not early vs late exposure.

source: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave & Ulrich (2026) AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Product Ideas (arXiv 2607.27553), Study 3b
finding: Fresh contexts with an identical prompt are the LEAST diverse arm. When each idea came from its own independent GPT-4o session, set diversity fell sharply, below one session writing many ideas. This reverses the S3 assumption that N fresh contexts beat one context.
numbers: Diversity = 1 minus average pairwise cosine similarity. GPT-4o independent sessions (1 idea per session) 0.452 [0.442,0.461]; GPT-4o zero-shot, one session listing many ideas 0.679 [0.670,0.688]; GPT-4o chain of thought (10 ideas per step, previous context kept) 0.698; humans 0.773 [0.764,0.782]; GPT-4 zero-shot 0.585. Task: product ideas for college students under $50.
limits: GPT-4o (Aug 2024), one task family, embedding-distance diversity, no quality score for this arm. Tokens were not matched: independent sessions cost more prompt overhead per idea.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on same-prompt fresh contexts for variety. Diversity needs either an in-context list (the model steers away from its own earlier items) or injected heterogeneity (see d07). Closes the diversity half of gap 1 for a GPT-class model; no Claude test here (but see d08).

source: Terwiesch et al. (2026) arXiv 2607.27553, Studies 3a-3c: personas, constraints, bold-refinement, scaling
finding: Injecting a random persona or a random design constraint per session (100 ideas per session, 20 sessions) nearly closes the diversity gap. Sonnets help little. Repeatedly making ideas bolder lowers diversity (a local-search trap). Making personas more eccentric did not raise diversity further. Scaling the pool from 100 to 1,000 ideas kept improving coverage of the human idea space with no plateau.
numbers: Diversity: random personas 0.757 [0.748,0.766]; random constraints 0.735; human-picked problem + AI solution 0.739; sonnets 0.686; bold-refinement agent (2 passes) 0.575 vs 0.679 plain. Coverage (mean nearest-neighbour distance from 200 human ideas to the LLM pool): 0.546 at N=100 to 0.478 at N=1,000; max distance 0.762 to 0.711. Model comparison (study 3a): DeepSeek R1 0.752, Claude Sonnet 3.5 0.682.
limits: Persona and constraint effects were measured on a creative product task with GPT-4o, not on proofs or code. Coverage is measured against human ideas, not against a correctness check. No dedupe-based stop rule.
agent_relevance: Persona or constraint diversification across fresh contexts works for open ideation (gap 5, ideation half closed). Iterative 'make it bolder' on the same ideas is anchoring on own output (gap 4): it lowered diversity. Pool scaling did not saturate at 1,000, which differs from Si et al. (d10).

source: Wadhwa, Narayanan Venkit, Hayashi, Li, Chakrabarty & Wu (2026) Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas (arXiv 2610.22324), Table 12 and Table 5
finding: First direct test on a Claude-class model. For Claude Opus 4.8, three independent single-idea samples were far less diverse than three ideas written in one response, but the one-response set lowered per-idea quality. Net utility changed little.
numbers: 1,740 test instances. Claude Opus 4.8: independent sampling (k=1, n=3) average distance 0.24, win rate vs gold 0.33, creative utility 0.34; set in one response (k=3, n=1) distance 0.80, win rate 0.21, utility 0.38. Closed models overall: distance rises from 0.24-0.53 to 0.79-0.86 with set prompting. Execution check on 132 ideas, success@3: Claude Opus 4.8 27%, trained 8B model 33%.
limits: Per-row labels in the extracted table are partly garbled; the Claude numbers are taken from the paper's own text. Task is NLP research ideas from paper context. Win rate is model-judged.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 for a Claude-class model: same-prompt fresh contexts collapse (distance 0.24) while a single context listing a set spreads (0.80), at a quality cost per idea (win rate 0.33 to 0.21). S3 should combine both: set-level listing inside each fresh context, then a selector, rather than many bare single-idea contexts.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Human-like Diversity (COLM 2025), arXiv 2504.05228, Sec 4 and App A.1
finding: In-context regeneration (keep all earlier answers in the conversation and ask for a different one) was the best prompting fix: Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro all roughly matched author-written human diversity over 8 generations. Paraphrasing and a system prompt asking for unique answers were only marginal. For reasoning models, more reasoning effort did not help: the OpenAI o3 and o3-mini results trend toward fewer distinct generations and lower utility at higher effort; Gemini 2.5 Flash showed minimal effect.
numbers: 100 curated prompts, 3 models, 8 generations each, 8 author humans as baseline. Reasoning-effort panel is a bar figure (distinct generations out of 10 in the low single digits, falling with effort for the OpenAI models); exact per-level values not reliably read from the text layer.
limits: Seeing earlier answers HELPED here because the instruction asked for something different. That is not anchoring without such an instruction. Reasoning trend seen in two OpenAI models only; one Gemini model flat.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 half-answered: showing a model its own earlier outputs plus 'give a different one' avoids repeats. More thinking did not buy diversity (OpenAI) or did nothing (Gemini). No Claude extended-thinking test exists in these sources.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (arXiv 2409.04109), Sec 3 and 7.1 (re-read)
finding: Re-read for gaps 4 and 8. The 4,000 seed ideas per topic were generated WITH the titles of all previously generated ideas appended to the prompt and an instruction to avoid repetition. Even so, the share of non-duplicates in each new bucket kept falling and the accumulated non-duplicate count plateaued.
numbers: Dedupe: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, duplicate if cosine above 0.8 to any earlier idea. About 5% non-duplicates, about 200 of 4,000 per topic. Prompt used 6 demonstration examples and 10 retrieved papers.
limits: Averaged over topics; the per-bucket curve is in a figure, no exact threshold given. The 0.8 cutoff was set by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: showing previous titles slowed but did not stop saturation. A practical stop rule is the new-non-duplicate rate per batch. The curve gives the shape but not a tested cutoff. Tension with d07: Terwiesch saw no plateau at 1,000 on a looser product task and a different measure.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (arXiv 2408.03314), Sec 6 and Fig 7
finding: Equal-budget test of sequential revisions (each conditioned on previous attempts) against independent parallel samples, with a verifier. Sequential revisions narrowly beat parallel overall. Easy questions did best with all-sequential; hard questions did best with a mix, because parallel samples cover different high-level approaches.
numbers: MATH, PaLM-2 revision model, 4 revision trajectories of length 64 per question; verifier best-of-N weighted and majority both favoured sequential at matched generation count. The best sequential-to-parallel ratio depends on budget and difficulty bin. Exact accuracies are in figures.
limits: Math with a learned verifier, PaLM-2, not ideation and not a Claude model. Measures accuracy, not diversity.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 with a verifier: parallel fresh samples suit hard problems with several approaches; sequential refinement suits easy ones. Supports a difficulty-gated restart operator, and shows the benefit depends on a verifier being present.

source: Xia, Wang, Huang & Liu (2026) Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search (arXiv 2606.29718), Tables 3, 5
finding: As agent context grows, models stop with 'give up' or uncertain wrong answers long before the window is full ('inconclusive search failures'), even on easy queries. Managing context (summaries, discarding old tool results, sub-agents) works because it lowers peak context length and sends the model back to exploration. This is a working agent analogue of a break or restart.
numbers: 4 open models, 3 benchmarks, max 100 turns, 5 repeats. Qwen3.5-397B on BrowseComp with a length-triggered summary: threshold 32K accuracy 57.7%, inconclusive failures 2.4%; 48K 50.6%, 7.2%; 64K 41.7%, 20.2%. A shorter threshold meant more tool calls. The best method depends on the model's agentic strength (sub-agent isolation best for the strong model; keep-latest with summary best for the weaker GLM-4.7).
limits: The failure type is premature stopping, not mental set. Closed models (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.4) were excluded because their reasoning traces are hidden.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 9: the nearest evidence that truncating or summarising context and continuing raises accuracy. Use a length threshold for the restart-with-summary operator. It does not show that fixation specifically drops.

source: Xia et al. (2026) arXiv 2606.29718, Sec 3.2 parallel sampling with behaviour-aware filtering
finding: Eight parallel trajectories, dropping those that end in give-up or uncertain answers before aggregation, gave a 2.6 to 4.9 point gain across three aggregation rules. On datasets with few inconclusive failures, plain parallel sampling matched or beat context management at the same tool-call budget.
numbers: Sampling number 8 for plain ReAct, 4 for context-managed agents (they use more tool calls). Gains largest on BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus. Example GLM-4.7 average column (fewest turns / minimum length / majority vote): 63.1/65.5/64.9 without filter, 68.0/68.8/69.4 with filter.
limits: The filter uses the model's own stated confidence; majority vote needs exact-match answers.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a cheap select rule is to drop low-confidence terminations, then vote. Filtering costs nothing, extra contexts cost tokens, so apply it before spawning more.

source: MUTATE benchmark authors (2026) Beyond One Path: Evaluating and Enhancing Divergent Thinking in Interactive LLM Agents (arXiv 2605.28465), Tables 1-2, Sec 3.4, 4
finding: Agents show a mechanism-shift failure on every model: when one solution principle is blocked they swap tools within the same mechanism instead of switching to a different one, and repeat the same mechanism after repeated failure. This is Einstellung-like in an agent. A switch operator that fires when failures on one target pass a threshold, generates candidates without convergence pressure, then selects, raised Claude Sonnet 4.6.
numbers: 56-scenario benchmark. Path discovery: Claude Sonnet 4.6 base 30/56 (53.6%) to ReDNA 41/56 (73.2%), +19.6 points; GPT-5.4 27/56 (48.2%) to 38/56 (67.9%), +19.7; human average 79.9%. Self-Refine lowered Claude's path discovery (53.6% to 44.6%). EscapeAgent baseline 66.1% for Claude.
limits: Interactive text-game tasks with a hidden mechanism; no rate for 'share of all agent errors that are mental set' is reported. Author names not extracted.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for gap 7: a threshold-triggered divergent-then-select switch beats generic self-critique on a Claude model. It supports a switch operator but does not give the share of errors due to mental set.

source: Alavi Naeini, Saqur, Saeidi, Giorgi & Taati (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Exploring Creative Problem Solving and Einstellung Effect with the OnlyConnect Wall Dataset (arXiv 2306.11167)
finding: Puzzle walls built with deliberate red herrings (items that fit a wrong group). GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 solved very few walls compared with human solvers. Performance rose a lot when red herrings were randomised or removed, which fits a fixation reading.
numbers: 494 walls. Human 285 of 494 solved (1,405 of 1,976 groups). GPT-4 solved 3 to 6 walls depending on shots (6 at 0-shot); connection F1 41 to 45 for the best few-shot setting vs human about 80% correct connections.
limits: Old models (gpt-4-0314); fixation is inferred from a red-herring dilution manipulation, not a within-model set-up paradigm; no Claude.
agent_relevance: Supports 'misleading cues lower LLM performance', the Einstellung analogue. Too old and too crude to give a rate for current agents.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa & Bernardo (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (arXiv 2502.04381)
finding: M-ARC: 100 questions built so that a familiar heuristic is the trap (Einstellung). Models of early 2025 did poorly and were overconfident.
numbers: Physicians 66% (SE 5.3%). Best models Gemini 1.5 Pro 50% and o1 48%. Larger models better calibrated but still overconfident.
limits: Medical QA, 100 items, author-written. It measures susceptibility, not a share of errors in multi-step agent runs.
agent_relevance: A paradigm that targets mental set in LLMs. For gap 7 this is the only direct Einstellung-style probe of models, but it is not an agent-error census.

source: Shidara, Prem, Kim, Podlasek, Liu, Alaa & Bernardo (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (arXiv 2601.11866)
finding: The same Einstellung probe (mARC) on later reasoning models, including Claude. Strong reasoning models reached physician level; the trap is largely avoided by reasoning.
numbers: 100 items; physicians 0.66 (95% CI 0.55-0.75, mean of 5). Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 [0.738-0.763] over 15 runs at highest reasoning effort. On the 20 items most physicians missed (human accuracy 36%), Claude 4.1 Opus was decisively correct on 55.0% [39.9, 80.0], decisively wrong on 25.0%, indeterminate 20.0%.
limits: Same 100 items, so contamination or tuning toward the set is possible; highest-effort setting only; multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 7: for current Claude with reasoning on, the Einstellung trap is weaker than in humans on this probe. A restart operator may matter more for long multi-step runs (d14) than for single answers.

source: Hu, Rostami & Thomason (2026) Expert Personas Improve LLM Alignment but Damage Accuracy: Bootstrapping Intent-Based Persona Routing with PRISM (arXiv 2603.18507)
finding: Expert personas help tone and alignment tasks but lower accuracy on knowledge and reasoning. Shorter personas hurt less; none removed the loss.
numbers: MMLU: no persona 71.6%; expert persona 68.0%; long persona 66.3%. On a dice problem a math persona answer was judged 1.5/10 where no persona was 9/10.
limits: Instruction-tuned and reasoning-distilled open models; MMLU is multiple-choice recall, not ideation.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: persona diversification has an accuracy price on correctness tasks. Keep personas short, and use them only where diversity is needed (strategy choice for proofs and code), with a verifier in the loop.

source: Ferreira, Liu, Zheng et al. (2026) Beyond Symmetric Agents: Cognitive Diversity and Multi-Agent Debate in Small Language Models (arXiv 2609.35875)
finding: Budget-matched test on correctness tasks. Diversity by persona, temperature or mixed models did not help. Persona prompting cost accuracy; the cost came from wearing personas at all, not from their diversity. Self-consistency sampling at the same budget matched or beat debate.
numbers: 23 open models, 5 tasks, 5,500+ runs. Maximally diverse persona teams vs plain debate: CSQA -2.1 to -4.4 points (p at most .005); biography precision -3.8 to -5.0. Near-clone personas -4.3 on GSM8K (p=.012); moving from most redundant to most diverse persona team changed accuracy by +2.9 on MMLU. Temperature spread: -0.11 to -0.41 points, all p at least .34. Mixed-model debate -1.04 [-1.61,-0.52] vs matched ensembles. Fixing context overflow alone moved debate vs sampling from -1.8 to parity.
limits: Small open-weight models, no Claude; correctness tasks with exact answers. Does not test creative breadth.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: on correctness tasks, persona diversity is not a free lever; plain independent samples plus a vote or verifier is the bar to beat. Also warns that transcript overflow can fake a diversity effect: check context limits before comparing arms.

source: Carichon, Sharma, Girard, Rampa & Farnadi (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs (arXiv 2606.00875)
finding: 25 prompts built from defixation and creativity methods (TRIZ, C-K, SCAMPER, brainstorming, design thinking, scenarios, plus 4 LLM-specific category-negation prompts) on 81 briefs expanded to 567 variants, 5 models. Simple 'think wild, go beyond obvious categories' prompts beat the elaborate method prompts. Homogenisation across models stayed.
numbers: 14,350 prompts; models GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-flash, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Grok-4.1-Fast. Best method prompts raised novelty by roughly 10 to 24 percent over control; top-5 idea rarity gains up to about 41 percent (read from a figure). Cross-model embedding distances only 0.206 to 0.341. Surprising attributes raised novelty at the cost of diversity.
limits: Single-shot; no example is shown to the model, so it does not test the example-fixation effect itself. Embedding-distance metrics; no Claude. Percent gains read from figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (LLM replication): no in-context flawed-example study was found. This is the nearest, and it says an explicit divergence instruction beats elaborate method prompts.

source: Wu, Goyal & Raghunathan (2025) Mode-Conditioning Unlocks Superior Test-Time Scaling (arXiv 2512.01127)
finding: Parallel sampling is limited by diversity collapse: repeated samples make the same mistakes. Spending the budget evenly across distinct reasoning modes (specialists or mode prefixes) beats drawing k samples from one mixed distribution. The argument is exact: with two modes of success p1 and p2, Pass@k with k/2 per mode beats the mixed draw.
numbers: Pass@k(std)=1-(1-p)^k; Pass@k(ModC)=1-(1-p1)^(k/2)(1-p2)^(k/2). Qwen2.5-7B with ModC: 4x efficiency gain on OpenThoughts; up to 10 percent gains on NuminaMath with gradient-clustered modes. Models 0.5B to 7B.
limits: Trained small models, math and graph search; no Claude. The gain needs modes that are complementary.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 on proofs and code: diversity serves correctness when it is mode coverage (different strategies) rather than persona flavour. A prefix naming the strategy (induction, contradiction, brute force) is the agent version.

source: Doudkin, Voelker & von Borries (2025) The Spark Effect: On Engineering Creative Diversity in Multi-Agent AI Systems (arXiv 2510.15568)
finding: Industry white paper: persona-conditioned agents raised a judged diversity score over a single generic-prompt agent.
numbers: gpt-5-mini baseline; mean diversity 3.14 vs 7.90 for ten curated personas (+4.76 in the table; the abstract says +4.1 for the finalised set); paired t(6)=7.61, p=2.68e-4, Cohen d=2.88 over 7 tasks; first persona version +0.61, p=.47, d=0.29. Score is 1-10 by a gpt-5 judge calibrated to human gold.
limits: Seven tasks, LLM judge, vendor paper with product interest, not peer-reviewed. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Terwiesch (d07): curated personas diversify. The first persona version did nothing, so persona quality matters.
